extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of American government and politics; scholars, reformers, and policymakers interested in state legislative procedure and reform
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of organization, procedure, defects, and proposed remedies for state legislatures (committee practice, bill processing, publicity rules, anti-lobby measures, drafting and reference services). Geared to understanding how to evaluate and improve legislative quality and process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of proposed special laws in local newspaper
rubrics_metrics.description: Require the publication of any proposed special law in a newspaper circulating in the locality affected, enabling citizens to take action upon the measure before it is passed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopted in Vermont, New York, Oklahoma and several other states as a device to give the community a right to pass upon laws applicable to it; recommended as a way to increase publicity and citizen action prior to passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-subject title requirement for bills
rubrics_metrics.description: Each bill must cover only one subject expressed clearly in the title to prevent the coupling of many vicious bills with a good one or the insertion of totally distinct matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common constitutional stipulation intended to secure regularity and to prevent 'log-rolling' or surprise insertions of unrelated provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments to existing statutes must clearly state exact change
rubrics_metrics.description: Former statutes may be amended only in such a way as to make clear the exact change that has been made in the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule intended to preserve clarity of statutory law and avoid confusion about the law's current state after amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of multiple readings and limits on late introductions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a common custom to require three different readings of every measure passed, and to prohibit the introduction of bills after the expiration of a certain part of the session to prevent rushing through pernicious measures during closing hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural protections aim to secure deliberation and publicity; in practice exceptions may be permitted by unanimous consent or governor's certification of necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed bills on members' desks prior to final passage; no last-minute amendments; record of yeas and nays
rubrics_metrics.description: No bill shall be passed or become a law unless it shall have been printed and upon the desks of the members in its final form at least three calendar legislative days prior to its final passage; at the last reading no amendment may be made; the question upon final passage must be taken immediately afterward, and the yeas and nays entered on the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example drawn from the New York constitution; designed to secure publicity and prevent last-minute alterations without opportunity for member or public review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee duty to consider measures and hear interests for and against
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the business of a legislative committee to consider carefully measures referred to it, and to hear the various interests for and against them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice only a few bills receive full treatment; statutes (e.g., New York) may authorize committees to require attendance of witnesses, issue commissions for out-of-state witnesses, pay witness fees, and pay expenses for investigations outside the capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee investigative powers and witness procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative committees may require the attendance of witnesses in the state, issue commissions for examination of out-of-state or absent witnesses, allow witnesses the same fees as civil court witnesses, and have their actual and necessary expenses paid when instructed to investigate outside the capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These powers facilitate thorough inquiry; in practice advocates and opponents often attend hearings as unpaid participants rather than formal witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public notice of hearings and impartial weighing of testimony (Massachusetts model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice of all hearings is given in the public press; committee meetings are well attended; testimony is carefully weighed and committees assume a judicial attitude — receiving petitions, testimony, and arguments to decide matters impartially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited as a high point of committee development: public notice, open hearings, and careful weighing of evidence help the legislature adapt work to concrete conditions and prevent hasty legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee system: expertise-building and public contact (value and risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee system enables a few members to become experienced in subjects; hearings bring arguments on both sides and indicate public demand, helping adaptation to social and economic conditions and preventing hasty legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Countervailing disadvantage: committees can smother good measures or carry pernicious measures without adequate scrutiny; committee choices and amendments may defeat original intents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaker's powers and caucus control
rubrics_metrics.description: In the majority party caucus the speaker is chosen and general measures to be carried are determined; the speaker usually appoints committees and, by distributing members judiciously, can secure predominance of friends on important committees and influence what measures come up for consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The caucus keeps party discipline; speakers or floor leaders (e.g., Merritt, Wadsworth example) can control calendars and the fate of bills, sometimes leading to organization dominance and suppression of independents' bills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal bill introduction, referral, reading, and committee report stages
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill is introduced by private member deposit, committee report, order of the house, or messenger from the senate; introduced bills are referred to committees; favorable committee reports lead to second reading and debate (section by section), then referral to revision and engrossing committees before third reading and placement on calendar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard sequence intended to structure deliberation; unanimous consent can advance bills; motions (e.g., to strike out enacting clause) reopen debate; rules and practices vary between houses and states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on debate and closure procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules may limit speaking (e.g., no member shall speak more than twice on one question without leave or more than fifteen minutes at a time except with two-thirds consent); debate can be closed by motion that the main question be put; in the senate, after six hours of consideration a closure motion is in order and, if approved, forces immediate vote with limited further debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules are intended to prevent unnecessary delay and ensure orderly progression of business while preserving minority rights in some measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of last-minute and unanimous-consent abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules intended to prevent advancing bills by unanimous consent out of order or introducing bills in closing days without proper notice, which can be used by the organization to control outcomes and bypass ordinary consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text documents common abuses: 'advancing by unanimous consent' subject to speaker recognition, 'gaveling' bills through, ignoring roll-call demands, pocketing reported bills so they arrive too late to pass — all undermine transparency and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for bills and limiting excessive legislative output
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedy the absence of responsibility (where any member may introduce unlimited bills without assuming responsibility) and reduce the excessive quantity of legislation to improve quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes of bad legislation include lack of responsibility, rushed sessions, log-rolling, and excessive prolixity; proposals include restricting bill introduction and measures to ensure members and executives have time to consider measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of competent bill drafters and technical drafting assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Appoint competent drafters whose duty is to draw bills, examine and revise proposed bills, and advise as to consistency and legal effect of legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: New York statute directing temporary senate president and speaker to appoint such drafters during sessions; in practice the experts are not always consulted, but their use is recommended to improve technical quality and fit with existing statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative reference library and expert reference staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish and maintain a legislative library and employ a legislative reference librarian to collect material bearing upon measures, keep records of state legislation, issue bulletins, and provide competent expert assistance to members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New York (legislative library established 1890) and Wisconsin (appropriated funds 1901 and employed Dr. McCarthy) demonstrate the value of ready access to legislative materials and expert economic/political analyses to improve legislative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office of revisor (statute consolidation and maintenance duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create an office of revisor with duties: (1) maintain a loose-leaf system of statutes separating in-force from repealed; (2) maintain a ledger of court decisions referring to statutes; (3) present bills for consolidation/revision to committees; (4) keep an alphabetical subject card-index to statutes; (5) formulate plans for order/classification/printing of statutes and session laws; (6) supervise preparation, printing, and binding of compilations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited Wisconsin (created 1909) as a model to bring order to statutory law and assist committees in consolidation and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-lobbyist registration and financial disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Require every person retained or employed for compensation to promote or oppose legislation to register annually in the office of the secretary of the state, give the name of the person or association retaining them, and furnish a brief description of the legislation they are working on; require persons or corporations to file a complete account of money spent influencing legislation during the immediately preceding session; impose penalties for noncompliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: New York statute exempts duly accredited agents of public bodies but imposes penalties on others; intended to reduce sinister private influence and increase transparency of lobbying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction of lobbyist activities to committee arguments and printed briefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibit legislative agents or counsels from attempting to influence members privately; require them to confine themselves to arguing before committees and filing printed briefs with members of the houses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wisconsin law noted as having a salutary effect: lobbyists 'disappeared' from corridors and hotels; the restriction reduced clandestine influence and discouraged social/barroom pressure on members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of special investigative committees/commissions to prepare technical measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Create special committees or commissions to investigate important technical problems thoroughly and prepare complete measures for the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable examples: New York's Stevens gas committee (1904) and Armstrong commission (1905) produced in-depth studies and furnished the basis for important reformatory legislation; recommended as a method to bring definite information to bear on legislative problems.
